patient.name: Desmond Clarke
patient.complaint: Weak right hand, dropping things and muscle twitching for 6 months
background: His father developed a personality change and dementia in his 60s
No diabetes; drinks 6 units a week

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with progressive asymmetric weakness, fasciculations and a mix of UMN and LMN signs with normal sensation and eye movements; distractors are myasthenia, MS, GBS and cervical myelopathy.

points: Desmond, 61: **can't turn keys** with his right hand.
Notices **twitching** in his arm and thigh muscles.

steps.lead: Progressive, painless weakness over months in a 61 year old: think **MND**, most often **ALS** with mixed UMN and LMN signs.

points: Right hand: **wasting** of first dorsal interosseous; **fasciculations**.

steps.lead: Desmond has **both** LMN signs (wasting, fasciculations) and UMN signs (brisk reflexes, Hoffmann's, Babinski) in the same limbs.

steps.q: Which finding makes MND more likely than cervical myelopathy for Desmond?
steps.r: Cervical myelopathy usually gives **sensory** signs. MND spares **sensation and eye movements**.

steps.lead: Normal sensation and eye movements are the **key distinguishing feature**; bulbar signs may follow.

head: Variant
Signs

rows: CN IX, X, XII: dysarthria, dysphagia, tongue fasciculations

steps.lead: Desmond's mixed signs fit **ALS**. His father's dementia raises the question of **familial ALS (C9orf72)**.

steps.text: Fasciculations + weakness is not myasthenia gravis: MG is **fatigable**, has no fasciculations and often affects the **eyes** (ptosis, diplopia).

steps.lead: Desmond needs his breathing and cognition watched: **respiratory failure** is the commonest cause of death and **FTD** is linked.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' where EMG/nerve conduction studies is the answer and MRI spine is the distractor used to exclude compression.

steps.q: Which test best supports the diagnosis of MND?
steps.r: **EMG/NCS** show widespread denervation with normal sensory conduction.

steps.title: Desmond's EMG / nerve conduction studies
steps.text: Widespread active denervation with normal sensory nerves: fits MND.

steps.lead: Desmond's EMG shows denervation in several regions with **normal sensory studies**: the gold-standard support for MND.
An **MRI cervical spine** is done to exclude cord compression; it does not diagnose MND.

steps.title: Bloods to exclude mimics
steps.text: Normal: no B12, calcium or thyroid mimic.

visual.label: Desmond 86%

steps.text: MRI does **not** diagnose MND; it rules out compressive or structural causes such as cervical myelopathy.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate treatment?' where riluzole is the disease-modifying drug, PEG is for dysphagia and weight loss, and NIV is for respiratory failure.

steps.q: Which drug slows Desmond's disease progression?
steps.r: **Riluzole** is the only first-line disease-modifying drug; steroids and IVIg do not help MND.

steps.lead: Desmond starts **riluzole**; it extends survival only modestly (historically about **3 months**).

points: Lost 8 kg; meals take an hour.

steps.lead: Desmond's MDT includes physio, **speech and language therapy** and dietetics; with weight loss and unsafe swallow he has a **PEG** placed.

visual.title: Desmond over 2 years
visual.caption: PEG at 14 months steadies weight; FVC keeps falling.

steps.title: Arterial blood gas on air
steps.text: Type 2 respiratory failure with metabolic compensation: chronic hypoventilation.

steps.lead: Desmond's hypercapnic respiratory failure is treated with **NIV**, which improves symptoms and survival.

science.exam: Expect applied questions on UMN vs LMN signs, why sensation is spared, C9orf72/SOD1 and TDP-43, and riluzole's anti-glutamate action.

steps.lead: Desmond is losing both **corticospinal (UMN)** neurons and **anterior horn cells (LMN)**.
Desmond's brisk reflexes come from lost **descending inhibition**; his wasting and twitching from **denervated** muscle fibres.

steps.q: Desmond's father had dementia with personality change. Which shared pathology links FTD and ALS?
steps.r: **C9orf72** repeat expansions link ALS and FTD through shared **TDP-43** pathology.

steps.lead: If Desmond carries a **C9orf72** hexanucleotide repeat, it would explain both his ALS and his father's FTD.

steps.title: Glutamate excitotoxicity
nodes: Excess glutamate at motor neuron synapses

steps.lead: Riluzole targets **glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity**, slowing Desmond's motor neuron loss a little.
Desmond's normal sensation and eye movements reflect sparing of **sensory pathways and oculomotor neurons**.

prompts.q: What is MND and what is its most common form?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: progressive, motor only, UMN plus LMN.

points.p: Progressive neurodegeneration of motor neurons in brain and spinal cord
points.why: Weakness and wasting over months to years.

points.p: ALS is the most common type
points.why: Spinal ALS is the commonest variant.

points.p: Mixed UMN and LMN signs
points.why: Both together in the same region is the clue.

prompts.q: List the UMN and LMN signs seen in MND.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name both sets in the same limb.

points.p: Asymmetric limb weakness
points.why: Often starts in one hand or foot.

points.p: UMN: spasticity, brisk reflexes, upgoing plantars (Babinski)
LMN: wasting, fasciculations, absent reflexes
Hoffmann's sign may be positive
points.why: Flicking the middle finger tip causes thumb flexion.

prompts.q: What is classically spared and what are the bulbar features?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: normal sensation and eyes separate MND from mimics.

points.p: Eye movements spared
Sensation spared
points.why: Sensory signs suggest myelopathy or neuropathy.

points.p: Bulbar: dysarthria, dysphagia, tongue fasciculations, weight loss

prompts.q: What are the MND variants and which has the worst prognosis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: classify by UMN, LMN or bulbar.

points.p: Progressive bulbar palsy (CN IX, X, XII): worst prognosis, ~2–3 years
Progressive muscular atrophy: LMN only
Primary lateral sclerosis: UMN only
Familial ALS: C9orf72 and SOD1
points.why: C9orf72 is the commonest familial cause.

prompts.q: What are the key complications and associations of MND?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: what kills, and what else to look for.

points.p: Respiratory failure: commonest cause of death
points.why: Watch FVC, orthopnoea and morning headache.

points.p: Frontotemporal dementia association

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: EMG diagnoses, MRI excludes.

points.p: EMG / nerve conduction studies: gold standard and first-line
points.why: Shows widespread denervation with normal sensory conduction.

points.p: MRI brain/spine to exclude structural or compressive causes

prompts.q: What is the disease-modifying treatment and how much does it help?

points.p: Riluzole (antiglutamatergic) first-line
points.why: The only first-line disease-modifier in the notes.

points.p: Slows progression; survival gain small (~3 months)

prompts.q: What supportive treatments are used as MND progresses?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: match each problem to its support.

points.p: Physiotherapy

prompts.q: Why do UMN and LMN signs differ, and why are eyes and sensation spared?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: which neuron is lost explains each sign.

points.p: UMN loss: spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski from lost descending inhibition
LMN loss: wasting, weakness, fasciculations from denervation
points.why: Anterior horn cells and cranial nerve nuclei.

points.p: Sensory pathways and oculomotor neurons spared

prompts.q: Which genes are implicated, why is FTD linked, and how does riluzole work?

points.p: C9orf72 hexanucleotide repeat expansion: commonest familial cause
points.why: Also found in some sporadic ALS.

points.p: Shared TDP-43 pathology links ALS and FTD
SOD1: toxic gain of function
Riluzole reduces glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity

glossary.MND: Motor neurone disease: progressive degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons.
glossary.ALS: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, the commonest form of MND with mixed UMN and LMN signs.
glossary.UMN: Upper motor neuron: from motor cortex down the corticospinal tract to the spinal cord.
glossary.LMN: Lower motor neuron: from anterior horn or cranial nerve nucleus to muscle.
glossary.fasciculations: Visible, irregular twitches of small groups of muscle fibres from denervation.
glossary.spasticity: Velocity-dependent increase in tone from UMN damage.
glossary.hyperreflexia: Abnormally brisk reflexes, a UMN sign.
glossary.Babinski: Upgoing big toe on stroking the sole, a UMN sign.
glossary.Hoffmann's sign: Thumb flexion when the middle finger tip is flicked, a UMN sign.
glossary.bulbar: Relating to the brainstem cranial nerves controlling speech and swallowing.
glossary.jaw jerk: Reflex closing of the jaw when the chin is tapped; tests the trigeminal pathway.
glossary.progressive bulbar palsy: MND variant affecting cranial nerves IX, X and XII, with the worst prognosis.
glossary.progressive muscular atrophy: MND variant with LMN signs only.
glossary.primary lateral sclerosis: MND variant with UMN signs only.
glossary.frontotemporal dementia: Dementia with early behaviour, personality or language change, linked to MND.
glossary.C9orf72: Gene whose hexanucleotide repeat expansion is the commonest genetic cause of ALS and FTD.
glossary.SOD1: Superoxide dismutase gene; mutations cause a subset of familial ALS.
glossary.TDP-43: A protein that aggregates in neurons in most ALS and many FTD cases.
glossary.hexanucleotide repeat: A six-base DNA sequence repeated many times, as in C9orf72.
glossary.EMG: Electromyography: recording muscle electrical activity to detect denervation.
glossary.NCS: Nerve conduction studies: measuring speed and size of nerve signals.
glossary.denervation: Loss of nerve supply to muscle fibres.
glossary.anterior horn cells: Lower motor neuron cell bodies in the spinal cord.
glossary.corticospinal tract: The main descending UMN pathway from cortex to spinal cord.
glossary.cervical myelopathy: Spinal cord compression in the neck causing UMN signs and sensory loss.
glossary.riluzole: Antiglutamatergic drug that modestly slows MND progression.
glossary.excitotoxicity: Nerve cell damage from excessive stimulation by glutamate.
glossary.glutamate: The main excitatory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system.
glossary.PEG: Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy: a feeding tube through the abdominal wall into the stomach.
glossary.NIV: Non-invasive ventilation through a tight-fitting mask, for hypercapnic respiratory failure.
glossary.FVC: Forced vital capacity: total air blown out after a full breath; falls with respiratory muscle weakness.
glossary.orthopnoea: Breathlessness lying flat; in MND a sign of diaphragm weakness.
glossary.type 2 respiratory failure: Low oxygen with high carbon dioxide from hypoventilation.
glossary.SALT: Speech and language therapy, assessing speech and swallow.
glossary.myasthenia gravis: Autoimmune neuromuscular junction disease with fatigable weakness, often of eye muscles.

technique.stem: A 58 year old man has 8 months of progressive weakness of his left hand and right leg. He has no pain or numbness. There is wasting and fasciculation of the left hand muscles, brisk reflexes in all limbs and upgoing plantars. Sensation and eye movements are normal.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about weakness: sort UMN vs LMN, then check sensation.

clues: Sensation and eye movements are normal
steps.x: LMN signs (wasting, fasciculations) plus UMN signs (brisk, Babinski), purely motor.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Mixed UMN + LMN, sensation and eyes spared: **ALS (MND)**.

elim: Usually gives sensory loss and neck pain; does not explain leg LMN-UMN mix with normal sensation.
Acute, ascending, areflexic; not 8 months with brisk reflexes.
Relapsing, with sensory and visual symptoms; no fasciculations.
Fatigable, often ocular; no wasting, fasciculations or UMN signs.

steps.x: **A. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.** Rule: UMN + LMN signs + normal sensation = MND.

technique.stem: A 64 year old woman has 6 months of progressive arm weakness with fasciculations, wasting and brisk reflexes. Sensation is normal. An MRI of the cervical spine shows no cord compression.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

steps.x: Diagnostic investigation after excluding compression.
Suspected MND with compression already excluded.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **EMG/NCS** is the gold standard.
**C. EMG and nerve conduction studies.** Rule: EMG diagnoses, MRI excludes.

technique.stem: A 67 year old man has recently been diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis after EMG. He can still walk and swallow normally. He asks if any medicine can slow the disease.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate drug?

steps.x: A disease-modifying drug question.
Confirmed ALS; wants disease modification.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Riluzole** slows progression modestly.

elim: For GBS or CIDP, not MND.

steps.x: **B. Riluzole.** Rule: MND disease-modifier = riluzole (small survival benefit).

technique.stem: A 49 year old man has ALS. His mother had frontotemporal dementia and his maternal uncle died of MND. Genetic testing is offered.
technique.q: Which is the most likely genetic abnormality?

steps.x: Genetics: link ALS and FTD in a family.
Familial ALS plus FTD in the family.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **C9orf72** repeat expansion links ALS and FTD (TDP-43).

elim: Spinal muscular atrophy, usually in childhood.
Causes some familial ALS but not the commonest and less linked to FTD.

steps.x: **A. C9orf72 hexanucleotide repeat expansion.** Rule: ALS + FTD family history = C9orf72.

practice.stem: A 63 year old man has 9 months of progressive weakness of his right arm. He has twitching in his arm and thigh muscles. There is wasting of the right hand, fasciculations, brisk reflexes and an upgoing left plantar. Sensation and eye movements are normal. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 76 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Progressive asymmetric weakness with mixed UMN and LMN signs and normal sensation is MND. Myasthenia is fatigable with no fasciculations.

steps.x: Diagnosis: UMN + LMN + sensation.

clues: Sensation and eye movements are normal
steps.x: Mixed UMN and LMN signs, sensory and eyes spared.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **MND (ALS)**.

elim: Sensory loss and areflexia, not brisk reflexes.
Myopathy; no UMN signs or fasciculations.
Sensory/visual relapses; fasciculations are not a feature.
Fatigable weakness without wasting or fasciculations.

steps.x: **C. Motor neurone disease.** UMN + LMN, no sensory loss = MND.

practice.stem: A 72 year old woman has 4 months of slurred speech and choking on liquids. She has lost 6 kg. Her tongue is wasted with fasciculations. Limb power is normal. Sensation and eye movements are normal. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Dysarthria, dysphagia and tongue fasciculations with normal limbs is progressive bulbar palsy, the MND variant with the worst prognosis.

steps.x: Diagnosis: name the MND variant.
Bulbar LMN signs (CN IX, X, XII) with limbs spared.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Progressive bulbar palsy**.

elim: Fatigable, with ptosis or diplopia; no wasting.
Dysphagia for solids first; no tongue fasciculations or dysarthria.
UMN only; no wasting or fasciculations.
LMN signs in the limbs, not isolated bulbar.

steps.x: **D. Progressive bulbar palsy.** Bulbar MND = worst prognosis (~2–3 years).

practice.stem: A 55 year old man has 1 year of progressive weakness of both legs. There is wasting, fasciculations and absent ankle reflexes. Plantars are downgoing and tone is reduced. Sensation is normal. Nerve conduction studies show normal sensory nerves.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Pure LMN signs (wasting, fasciculations, areflexia) with no UMN signs is progressive muscular atrophy. ALS needs UMN signs as well.

steps.x: Diagnosis: name the MND variant.

clues: wasting, fasciculations and absent ankle reflexes
steps.x: LMN signs only, no UMN signs, sensory sparing.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Progressive muscular atrophy**.

elim: Needs UMN signs too; there are none.
Acute onset over days to weeks.
UMN only; this is LMN only.

steps.x: **E. Progressive muscular atrophy.** LMN only = PMA; UMN only = PLS.

practice.stem: A 60 year old woman is diagnosed with ALS after 8 months of progressive limb weakness with fasciculations and brisk reflexes. She is examined by a medical student.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
practice.e: Eye movements and sensation are characteristically spared in MND; ptosis suggests myasthenia.

steps.x: Most likely finding in MND.
MND: what is characteristically spared?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Eye movements** (and sensation) are spared.
**D. Normal eye movements.** MND spares eyes and sensation.

practice.stem: A 68 year old man with ALS for 2 years has orthopnoea, morning headaches and daytime sleepiness. His respiratory rate is 26 breaths per minute, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 132/78 mmHg and oxygen saturation 90% breathing air. Investigations are shown.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
practice.e: Orthopnoea, morning headaches and hypercapnia with a low FVC mean respiratory muscle weakness, the commonest cause of death in MND.

steps.x: Most likely cause in known MND.

clues: orthopnoea, morning headaches and daytime sleepiness
steps.x: Hypercapnia with compensation, low FVC: chronic hypoventilation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Respiratory muscle weakness** causing type 2 respiratory failure.

elim: No fever or focal chest signs; gas shows chronic compensation.
No oedema or crackles; normal BNP.
PE gives hypocapnia, not chronic hypercapnia.
Does not explain the low FVC and orthopnoea.

steps.x: **D. Respiratory muscle weakness.** Respiratory failure is the commonest cause of death in MND.

practice.stem: A 59 year old man with ALS has become disinhibited, makes inappropriate jokes and eats compulsively. His wife says his personality has changed over a year. His memory for recent events is relatively preserved.
practice.q: Which is the most likely associated diagnosis?
practice.e: Frontotemporal dementia is an important association of MND, presenting with disinhibition and personality change before memory loss.

steps.x: Association of MND.
Behavioural change with spared memory in ALS.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Frontotemporal dementia** (shared TDP-43).

elim: Low mood and withdrawal, not disinhibition.

steps.x: **D. Frontotemporal dementia.** ALS + behaviour change = FTD.

practice.stem: A 61 year old man has progressive hand weakness with wasting, fasciculations and brisk reflexes. Sensation is normal. His creatine kinase is mildly raised. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 130/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
practice.e: EMG and nerve conduction studies are the gold-standard investigation in MND, showing denervation with normal sensory conduction.

steps.x: Diagnostic investigation for suspected MND.
Suspected MND; CK rise is from denervation, not myopathy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **EMG/NCS**.

elim: For myopathy; a mildly raised CK is common in MND.
Supports multifocal motor neuropathy but does not diagnose MND.

steps.x: **C. EMG and nerve conduction studies.** MND gold standard = EMG/NCS.

practice.stem: A 57 year old woman has 6 months of weakness and stiffness in both legs with brisk reflexes and upgoing plantars, and fasciculations in her arms. She also has neck stiffness. MND is suspected.
practice.q: Which investigation is most important to exclude a structural cause?
practice.e: MRI brain/spine excludes structural or compressive causes such as cervical myelopathy; it does not diagnose MND.

steps.x: Investigation to exclude a mimic.
Cervical myelopathy can mimic mixed signs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **MRI cervical spine** excludes compression.

elim: Diagnoses MND but does not exclude compression.

steps.x: **E. MRI cervical spine.** MRI excludes; it does not diagnose MND.

practice.stem: A 66 year old woman with MND has slurred speech and coughs when drinking. She has lost 9% of her body weight over 3 months. A swallow assessment shows aspiration. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: PEG gives long-term nutritional support in MND with dysphagia and weight loss.

steps.x: Management of dysphagia and weight loss in MND.
Unsafe swallow with significant weight loss.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Long-term feeding: **PEG tube**.

elim: Poorly tolerated long term; PEG is preferred.
Gut works; enteral feeding is preferred.
Not enough with major weight loss and aspiration.

steps.x: **C. PEG tube.** MND dysphagia + weight loss = PEG.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man with ALS has orthopnoea and morning headaches. His respiratory rate is 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air. Investigations are shown.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: NIV is used for respiratory failure in advanced MND. High-flow oxygen alone risks worsening hypercapnia.

steps.x: Management of respiratory failure in MND.
Type 2 respiratory failure from muscle weakness.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

steps.x: **D. Non-invasive ventilation.** MND hypercapnic respiratory failure = NIV.

practice.stem: A 62 year old woman with newly diagnosed ALS has mild slurring of speech but swallows normally. Her weight is stable. She is worried about losing her voice.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate referral now?
practice.e: Supportive care includes speech and language therapy for dysarthria; PEG and NIV are for later dysphagia and respiratory failure.

steps.x: Supportive management matched to the problem.
Early dysarthria only.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Speech and language therapy**.

elim: Not yet; swallow and weight are normal.

steps.x: **E. Speech and language therapy.** Each problem gets its support: speech → SALT, swallow + weight → PEG, breathing → NIV.

practice.stem: A 60 year old man with ALS starts riluzole. He asks how it works. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of action?
practice.e: Riluzole is antiglutamatergic, reducing glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity that contributes to motor neuron death.

steps.x: Drug mechanism.
Antiglutamatergic drug.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Riluzole **reduces glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity**.

elim: SOD1 gain of function is a cause, not a drug target here.

steps.x: **E. Reduces glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity.** Riluzole = antiglutamate.
